newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crew saw "two fireballs" in India crash.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crew saw "two fireballs" in India crash.

text.p: A U.S. Air Force pilot said on Tuesday that he and members of his cargo-plane crew saw "two fireballs" plunge from the sky within about a minute after two civilian airliners collided near New Delhi.

"In the distance off our right-hand side, two fireballs seemed to appear ... diverging away from each other," the pilot told reporters at the Pentagon by telephone from India. "The two fireballs proceeded to descend down and hit the ground and became fireballs on the ground."
The pilot of the Air Force C-141 cargo plane, which was about 30 minutes from New Delhi on a landing approach at dusk when the tragedy occurred, declined to provide his identity.
An estimated 350 people were feared dead in the collision of a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet and a Kazakhstan airliner west of New Delhi.

The U.S. pilot said in response to questions from reporters that the collision of the two airliners occurred about 50 miles 80 km from his aircraft and that the fireballs quickly plunged from the sky.

"It was not very long. It was within a minute's time that it appeared that the fireballs came from beneath where we saw them emerge from the cloud and when they appeared to hit the ground and become just fire on the ground," he said.

The U.S. pilot said he and his crew did not see the actual collision, but did see a bright glow in cloud cover which they thought was lightning until ground controllers began sending radio queries to planes in the area.

"When we saw the fireballs coming away from the cloud the other pilot (aboard the Air Force plane) queried the (ground) controller who didn't have a response for us but began to inquire about other aircraft in the area without response," he said.
"We were number one (in the landing queue) into the airfield, so we proceeded uneventfully into the airport and landed."
The American pilot said that his aircraft was about 50 miles (80 km) northwest of New Delhi and headed southeast into New Delhi when they saw the glow in the clouds.
His aircraft landed about 30 minutes after he and members of his crew in the control cabin saw the glow, the pilot added.
At the State Department, spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters the United States was following the unfolding story of the crash with "horror and interest."
He said the U.S. Embassy in New Delhi was working very hard with Indian authorities to verify whether Americans were on either aircraft.
"We think it may be likely Americans might have been aboard the Saudia aircraft ... but we don't know that," Davies said.
